correctness.rationale: On each standard base chart normalize a weight-one coordinate to 1 and write zt=−f(s). Away from the two coordinate points this surface is smooth (a simultaneous zero of z,t is over a simple root, where f' is nonzero). Near p_z the cover z=1 is smooth with coordinates x,y and scalar μ_a action. Blow up the origin on the cover and take the quotient; a chart uses s=y/x and U=x^a, giving U=1/z in the normalized x=1 coordinates and t=−f(s)U. The quotient chart is smooth, and its zero section has normal bundle O(−a). The same construction at p_t gives V=1/t and z=−f(s)V, with section normal O(−b). The two resolutions are minimal because a,b≥2. Together with the affine equation, the charts give the map to the base and identify both sections. To check the first blow-down directly, use t as fiber coordinate of O(b), adding its infinity section to get F_b. The affine chart zt=−f(s) and the chart t=−f(s)U, with U=1/z on the overlap, are precisely the charts of the blow-up of the ideal (t,f(s)). The p_t chart makes the map an isomorphism near infinity. Thus one blows up exactly the d distinct reduced centers on the positive zero section, off the negative infinity section. At each center the total transform of its fiber is the proper transform plus the exceptional curve, both of square −1, meeting once and transversely. The exceptional component meets the proper transform of the zero section E_z and is the one contracted to F_b. Interchanging z,t gives the other model; the section squares satisfy −a+d=b and −b+d=a. The standard smooth blow-up formulas give Picard rank 2+d and canonical square 8−d. This proof is geometric. The inspected but unexecuted frozen script tests arithmetic identities only, and no numerical check is needed to establish the blow-ups. Repeated roots and a=1 are excluded.
